tier_reason: Discussion #361 has pgaskin's raw go test output (2026-03-10) and ncruces's benchstat of it (2026-03-18) with Go 1.26.0, the exact command, CPU Intel Core Ultra 7 258V and the go-marisa commits for both sides; the benchmark code (go-marisa BenchmarkTrie) and the Wasm build flags (src/Dockerfile at each commit) are public, so the run is reproducible.

corrections.baseline: wazero v1.10.1 (go-marisa's wazero-based bindings at commit 37cde21, Wasm blob built with -msimd128; wazero execution mode not stated on the page)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.26 (go1.26.0): CGO_ENABLED=0 go1.26.0 test -v -run='^$' -bench=BenchmarkTrie -count=6 in github.com/pgaskin/go-marisa. The two hashes on the page are go-marisa commits, not wasm2go/wazero commits: wasm2go side = go-marisa 075b64a04783d6c188ac9f66ea52688bc71edb9e ('mmap wip'; its src/Dockerfile pins wasm2go ecc45fd41abc75bace101eb275d9cb7c72aa76c4 and builds the Wasm with wasi-sdk 29 clang++ -O3 -mmutable-globals -mbulk-memory -mmultivalue -mnontrapping-fptoint -msign-ext, no SIMD, plus wasm-opt -O3 --gufa --converge); wazero side = go-marisa 37cde21a937175ff0928e5e6035b00a08be91daa (go.mod wazero v1.10.1; Wasm built with the same flags plus -msimd128 and wasm-opt --enable-simd).
corrections.caveats: Mixed result on one workload and one machine: queries, WriteTo, ReadFrom (-7.74%) and PredictiveSearchSeq (-15.19%) are faster, while Build (+16.46% Words, +34.67% Go125), UnmarshalBinary (+96.16%) and LookupAvg (+5.67%) are slower, so the -15.45% geomean hides regressions up to +96%. The raw runs are pgaskin's (go-marisa author, not the wasm2go author); the benchstat summary was posted by ncruces, the wasm2go author. The two sides are not the same Wasm blob: the wazero side's blob was built with SIMD128 and the wasm2go side's without SIMD, from a different (work-in-progress 'mmap wip') go-marisa commit with imported memory, so the comparison is binding-versus-binding rather than engine-versus-engine on identical input; ncruces attributes the Build regression to that 'SIMD-heavy part'. The go-marisa README now summarises the switch from wazero (v1.0.2 and older) as 'slightly faster at querying, but about 50% slower at building/reading/writing tries'. Not the go-sqlite3 workload that the discussion is about. Separate project from goccy/wasm2go.

notes: Numbers match ncruces's benchstat table in discussion #361 (geomean 109.5us to 92.58us, -15.45%; Go125/Lookup -27.34%; Words/ReverseLookup -40.45%; Words/WriteTo -77.68%; Build and UnmarshalBinary slower). Record called the go-marisa commit hashes wasm2go/wazero commits and said the wazero version was unstated; corrected to wazero v1.10.1 from go.mod at 37cde21. Shortcomings: mixed result with regressions up to +96%, wazero side ran a SIMD-built blob while the wasm2go side did not, wazero not one of the category's listed baselines.

tier_reason: First-party n-body README in AssemblyScript/examples gives 1606 ms (AS Wasm) vs 11640 ms (JS) vs 1611 ms (Rust Wasm) with public code, asconfig and Node flags, but no CPU model (only 'MacBook Pro (15-inch, 2019)'), an unpinned asc version ('latest') and an ambiguous step count, so it falls short of A; the independent LeanyLabs micro-benchmarks are a 7-star repo with mixed results, not a well-known suite.

corrections.caveats: The compiler repository itself carries no benchmark numbers (README and tests contain none) and the project's website could not be opened. The only first-party number is one n-body example in the separate AssemblyScript/examples repo: single workload, unspecified CPU model, asc version 'latest' (package.json devDependency), and Node started with --nowasm-bounds-checks --nowasm-stack-checks --noliftoff, which favours the Wasm side. The README says 'npm test [steps=1000000]' while tests/index.js defaults to 20000000 steps, and the table does not say whether it is the cold or warmed-up series. The JavaScript side is the AssemblyScript source transpiled by tsc (unchecked() calls stripped), not an idiomatic JS n-body, and its 11640 ms looks anomalous: AssemblyScript issue 1326 (June 2020, AssemblyScript 0.10.0, Node 14.4.0, Windows 10, 20,000,000 steps) measured the same sample at JavaScript 3.0 s and AssemblyScript 5.6 s, the opposite result. Independent micro-benchmarks (LeanyLabs/assemblyscript-benchmarks, 7 stars, i5-8250, assemblyscript ^0.18.4, Node version not stated) show JavaScript winning four of six cases. A 2020 Iowa State University master's creative component ('Benchmarking AssemblyScript for Faster Web Applications', Ostrich suite numerical kernels on Chrome and Firefox) reportedly finds 1.1x to 7.2x speedups over JavaScript (search snippet only; host blocked; not peer-reviewed). The baseline is JavaScript running on V8, not another Wasm runtime; the emscripten C++ baseline from the lead was not found for this project.

notes: n-body README numbers match (1606/11640/1611 ms; 7.2x derived), LeanyLabs ops/s match. Licence Apache-2.0, ~18k stars, last commit 2026-07-21 all verified. Shortcomings: single first-party workload with no CPU model and unpinned compiler, Wasm-favouring Node flags, JS baseline is a tsc transpile whose time is 4x slower than an earlier report, and independent micro-benchmarks mostly favour JavaScript.

tier_reason: Third-party gist (tong, created 2018-06-28) states the CPU and OS but no Haxe, HashLink or Neko versions, and its targets (cs, java, lua, php, python) are not in the in-repo other/benchs/Benchs.hx, so the script that produced it is not public; a personal gist is not a well-known suite, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party gist run of that suite (created 2018-06-28, Intel Core i5-6600, Arch Linux, kernel 4.17.2): total hl 5.68 s versus neko 27.16 s, 4.8x faster (derived from page data); per test Fib 0.08 vs 0.42 s, NBodies 0.13 vs 5.91 s, Anonymous 0.29 vs 4.57 s, Mandelbrot 4.28 vs 9.65 s. Same table: Haxe Lua target 60.55 s, Python target 48.73 s, PHP 12.59 s (hl about 10.7x, 8.6x and 2.2x faster, derived). Gist author's 2025-09-20 rerun on AMD Ryzen 7 7700: Fib hl 0.04 vs neko 0.58 s, Mandelbrot 1.32 vs 8.83 s (hlc column errored on every test). Slower than the other targets in the 2018 table: C++ 0.72 s, Java 0.81 s, JavaScript 0.96 s total.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-6600 @ 3.9 GHz, 15959 MB, Arch Linux, kernel 4.17.2 (2018 run); AMD Ryzen 7 7700, 32 GB, Arch Linux kernel 6.16.8 (2025 rerun)
corrections.caveats: The README has no numbers. The in-repo benchmark suite (other/benchs/Benchs.hx: hl, hlc, js, neko, cpp and swf/AIR targets) has no committed results; the figures come from a personal gist by a Haxe community member (created 2018-06-28, not 2016) whose table also has cs, java, lua, php and python targets that the in-repo script does not build, so the exact script is not published and tool versions are not stated; tier stays C. The 'Lua' and 'Python' columns are Haxe compiled to those targets, not hand-written Lua 5.x or CPython. HashLink loses to hxcpp, JVM and Node in the same table (Mandelbrot 4.28 s vs 0.10 s for JavaScript); in the 2025 rerun every hlc (HashLink/C) cell is an error ('hlc result 0 but expected'). A second repository (haddock7/hashlink_benchmark, i7-7500U, HashLink 1.11.0, OpenSimplex noise) has HashLink VM 16.76 s, HashLink/C 5.91 s, native C 3.88 s, i.e. HL VM 4.32x slower than native C. Haxe's 'HashLink InDepth' blog (haxe.org, blocked here) reportedly says HL/JIT beats Adobe AIR and Node/V8 in many cases (search snippet only), which the gist's numbers do not support for Node. NekoVM is not one of the category's listed baselines (wasmtime, wasmer, WAMR, V8).

notes: Gist numbers match the record; the gist was created 2018-06-28 (revisions page), not 2016, and the 2025 rerun is the gist author's own comment. Licence MIT, 905 stars, last commit 2026-10-06 verified. Shortcomings: only a personal gist with unstated versions and an unpublished modified script, baseline NekoVM is off the category list, HashLink is slower than hxcpp/JVM/Node, hlc errored in the 2025 rerun.
